summary.title: Writing a Linux Debugger Part 4: Elves and Dwarves
summary.one_liner: You learn how ELF sections and DWARF debug info (line tables and DIEs) map machine addresses to source lines, functions and variables, which a debugger needs for breakpoints and variable reads.
keywords: system v x86_64 abi frame pointer
takeaways: ELF is the object file format that stores code, data, debug info and tells the loader how to load the binary.
DWARF's .debug_line table maps code addresses to file, line and column, and works in both directions for breakpoints and stack location.
DWARF .debug_info is a tree of DIEs (tags plus attributes) describing compile units, functions, variables and types.
Finding a function from a PC means checking compile unit and function low_pc/high_pc ranges; breakpoints can skip the prologue using the prologue-end line entry.
Variables are read by evaluating DW_AT_location relative to the frame base, then interpreting bytes using the type DIE.
summary.summary: This is part 4 of a series on writing a Linux debugger in C++. It explains ELF as the Linux object file format and DWARF as the debug information format that links ELF binaries to source code. The article walks through a small example program, showing dwarfdump output for the line table and the .debug_info DIE tree. It then applies this to practical tasks: finding the function containing a PC, setting a breakpoint on a function while skipping the prologue, and reading a variable using its location and frame base. It also notes GCC and Clang differences and says a library will be used in later parts.
